The Rise of AI in PRC Influence Operations: Nine Takeaways from the GoLaxy Documents

Executive Summary

Recently leaked documents provide details into the PRC's efforts to develop fully autonomous AI-powered Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) systems. The systems can detect regional political trends, determine targets, generate content, and automatically deliver it through an army of realistic inauthentic accounts. Our review and additional analysis discovered seven account handles that we believe to be operated by GoLaxy. The documents disclose a list of GoLaxy's partners, customers, and ongoing projects. This provides a unique insight into the wider PRC FIMI infrastructure. The documents contain comprehensive monitoring plans for Taiwan.

Introduction

PRC FIMI has long been characterized as sloppy and easy to detect. Spamouflage accounts tend to have similar names and profile photos, use excessive copy-pasta, and are often active during PRC working hours. GoLaxy (中科天玑) aims to do just that. GoLaxy is a company that spinned off from the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (ICT CAS). A recent leak of internal documents, first exposed by researchers at Vanderbilt University and featured in the New York Times, uncovers some of the internal workings of the company. The GoLaxy Documents are 399 pages long and contain a wide collection of sales pitches, powerpoint presentations, and internal meeting minutes.

1: A comprehensive, holistic, turnkey solution — GoPro

The document appears to be a speech or sales pitch that introduces the "GoLaxy Smart Propaganda System GoPro". It appears to be written by the GoLaxy team at the Institute of Computing Technology (ICT) and is addressed to the higher leadership of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. According to the authors, the PRC has been facing continued US-orchestrated influence operations about Hong Kong, Xinjiang, COVID-19, and the trade war. As a result, Xi Jinping has made several calls to "strengthen frontline awareness, dare to speak out, and dare to 'unsheathe the sword' to seize the initiative in the online public opinion sphere as quickly as possible." This has directly led to a dedicated team of 50 members to establish a smart propaganda system. The piece ends by saying that this is only the first step of a "Long March" and admitting the team still needs to overcome some difficulties. They hope to strengthen their cooperation with the Cyberspace Administration of China, the Central Propaganda Department, the Science and Technology Commission of the Central Military Commission, and the Ministry of State Security.

2: Specific accounts mentioned in the GoLaxy documents

We are certain that these accounts are actually operated by the GoLaxy team and are not screenshots of random accounts, as two of them are followed or befriended by the personal social media accounts of GoLaxy engineers whose names and photographs also appear elsewhere in the documents. These accounts — or as the company calls them, 'persona bots' (拟人化机器人账号) — are presented as part of the final step in GoLaxy's system: automated smart posting. A look at these four accounts shows that they are clearly in an early stage. The accounts' posts are similar to standard Spamouflage content. The accounts' link to the PRC is obvious because of their use of simplified Chinese characters and, in some cases, overt pro-PRC propaganda. The accounts have several posts that are targeted at Taiwan.

4: GoLaxy's partners

We already knew that GoLaxy has received funding from Sugon, a PLA linked company. The documents contain a handout for a meeting held in December 2022. The meeting concerns an open research project on conducting FIMI operations in Taiwan. Xiamen Meiya Pico Information Security is a state-owned cybersecurity company controlled by the State Development and Investment Corporation (SDIC). It was added to the US Entity List in October 2019 for contributing to human rights abuses in Xinjiang. Hefei IFLY Digital Technology (also known as IFflytek Digital) is a subsidiary of the partially state-owned IFlytek. Similar to Meiya Pico, the company was added to the US Entity List in October 2019. Beijing Zhongke Ruijian Technology is also a partially state-owned company. Similar to GoLaxy, it is a spin-off from the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (ICT CAS). China digital Video is a privately owned company that develops technology products and provides technical support for the media industry. The company has collaborations with some of the most important PRC state media outlets such as the China Media Group and the Guangming Daily.

5: GoLaxy's Customers

Page 379 contains an overview of GoLaxy's ongoing projects and customers. The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) is the PRC's cyberspace regulator, overseeing both cyberspace security and internet content regulation. The Science and Technology Department of the Central Military Commission (CMC STC) seeks to strengthen and promote technological innovation for military purposes. Base 311 (also known as PLA Unit 61716) is a military base in Fuzhou that oversees the PRC's psychological warfare against Taiwan. The Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) is the PRC's agency that is responsible for cross-strait relations.

6: Targeting of Taiwan

GoLaxy's leaked documents show a granular, data-driven targeting program against Taiwan that combines large-scale political profiling, network mapping of elites and organizations, and election-focused opinion monitoring to support tailor-made influence and division campaigns. Beyond individuals, GoLaxy maintains a "Taiwan knowledge graph" (涉T知识图谱) that fuses data on Taiwan's political parties and institutions into a structured knowledge graph. The graph covers mainstream and smaller parties, including the Democratic Progressive Party, Kuomintang, Taiwan People's Party, New Party, Non-Partisan Solidarity Union, and others. The leak includes a weekly Taiwan online opinion report (台湾地区网络舆情周报) covering the late-2023 election period, before the 2024 general election. One report for 25 November — 1 December 2023 tracks 634,448 pieces of content, and follows the narrative competition among the DPP, KMT, and TPP presidential tickets treating them as the three main camps.

Concluding remarks

The GoLaxy documents highlight the PRC's reliance on companies and the tech community to conduct its FIMI operations. In recent weeks, there was another major leak containing audio files that discussed how another PRC tech company, Warming High-Tech (沃民高新科技), may have played a role in the 2018 mayoral elections in Kaohsiung. Taiwan's National Security Bureau also mentioned several other companies in a recent report.
